/-!
# Outer billiards

Outer billiards is a dynamical system defined relative to a convex shape $P$ in the plane.
For a point $x$ outside $P$, the outer billiards map sends $x$ to the point $y$ such that the
segment from $x$ to $y$ is tangent to $P$ at its midpoint and $P$ lies to the right of the ray
from $x$ to $y$. Equivalently, $y$ is the reflection of $x$ through the point where the right
support line from $x$ touches $P$. When $P$ is a polygon, the map is undefined at the points $x$
whose right support line meets $P$ along a side. The (two-sided) orbit of a point $x$ is the
sequence obtained by iterating the map and its inverse; it is well defined when every iterate is
defined, which is the case for almost every point.

An orbit is *bounded* if it is contained in some bounded region of the plane, and *unbounded*
otherwise. An orbit is *periodic* if it eventually repeats. Since the outer billiards map is
injective where it is defined, a well-defined orbit eventually repeats if and only if it is
periodic in the usual sense.

The Wikipedia list of unsolved problems in mathematics records "many problems concerning an
outer billiard, for example showing that outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon
have unbounded orbits". This file states this problem and the second open problem from the
open-problems section of the Wikipedia article on outer billiards: outer billiards relative to a
regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Outer billiard*, Open questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. E. Schwartz, *Unbounded orbits for outer billiards I*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702073)
- [S. Tabachnikov, *A proof of Culter's theorem on existence of periodic orbits in polygonal outer billiards*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1003)
-/

def rightSupportPoints (P : Set ℝ²) (x : ℝ²) : Set ℝ² :=
  {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0}
blocks.docstring:
The points of `P` lying on the right support line from `x`: the points `v ∈ P` such that
all of `P` lies (weakly) to the right of the ray from `x` through `v`.

Here "to the right" is measured with the standard orientation of the plane: `p` lies to the right
of the ray from `x` through `v` when the signed area `areaForm (v - x) (p - x)` is nonpositive.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib exposed-point/supporting-hyperplane material (e.g. `Set.exposedPoints`, `ConvexCone`, `IsExposed`) and `Orientation.areaForm`; none give the right-hand support line from a point. areaForm is used inside the definition.
justification.name: OuterBilliard.rightSupportPoints
justification.why_needed: Mathlib has no notion of support lines/tangent lines from an exterior point to a convex body with a prescribed side; needed to express 'the segment is tangent to P at its midpoint with P on the right' and the undefinedness when the tangency is along an edge.

blocks.name: rightSupportPoints
blocks.text:
/--
The points of `P` lying on the right support line from `x`: the points `v ∈ P` such that
all of `P` lies (weakly) to the right of the ray from `x` through `v`.

Here "to the right" is measured with the standard orientation of the plane: `p` lies to the right
of the ray from `x` through `v` when the signed area `areaForm (v - x) (p - x)` is nonpositive.
-/
def rightSupportPoints (P : Set ℝ²) (x : ℝ²) : Set ℝ² :=
  {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0}

blocks.code:
def IsStep (P : Set ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  x ∉ P ∧ ∃ v, rightSupportPoints P x = {v} ∧ y = Equiv.pointReflection v x
blocks.docstring:
`IsStep P x y` means that `y` is the image of `x` under the outer billiards map relative to `P`:
`x` lies outside `P`, the right support line from `x` touches `P` in exactly one point `v`, and
`y` is the reflection of `x` through `v`. When the right support line from `x` meets `P` along a
segment, the outer billiards map is undefined at `x` and `IsStep P x y` fails for every `y`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib function iteration and Euclidean reflection APIs; these concern total functions or reflection in affine subspaces and do not provide the partial outer-billiard map.
justification.name: OuterBilliard.IsStep
justification.why_needed: Models the polygonal outer-billiard map as genuinely partial at singular support lines and specifies reflection through the unique support vertex.

blocks.name: IsStep
blocks.text:
/--
`IsStep P x y` means that `y` is the image of `x` under the outer billiards map relative to `P`:
`x` lies outside `P`, the right support line from `x` touches `P` in exactly one point `v`, and
`y` is the reflection of `x` through `v`. When the right support line from `x` meets `P` along a
segment, the outer billiards map is undefined at `x` and `IsStep P x y` fails for every `y`.
-/
def IsStep (P : Set ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  x ∉ P ∧ ∃ v, rightSupportPoints P x = {v} ∧ y = Equiv.pointReflection v x

blocks.code:
def IsOrbit (P : Set ℝ²) (o : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, IsStep P (o k) (o (k + 1))
blocks.docstring:
`IsOrbit P o` means that the two-sided sequence `o : ℤ → ℝ²` is a well-defined outer
billiards orbit relative to `P`: for every `k`, the point `o (k + 1)` is the image of `o k`
under the outer billiards map. Such an orbit is determined by any one of its points.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib's `Function.IsPeriodicPt`/`Function.periodicOrbit` and iterate machinery assume a total map, which the outer billiards map is not; `Function.Periodic` is reused for periodicity.
justification.name: OuterBilliard.IsOrbit
justification.why_needed: Two-sided well-defined outer billiards orbit `o : ℤ → ℝ²` (each consecutive pair related by Step); needed for 'unbounded orbit' and 'periodic orbit'.

blocks.name: IsOrbit
blocks.text:
/--
`IsOrbit P o` means that the two-sided sequence `o : ℤ → ℝ²` is a well-defined outer
billiards orbit relative to `P`: for every `k`, the point `o (k + 1)` is the image of `o k`
under the outer billiards map. Such an orbit is determined by any one of its points.
-/
def IsOrbit (P : Set ℝ²) (o : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, IsStep P (o k) (o (k + 1))

noncomputable def regularPolygon (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun k : Fin n =>
    c + r • !₂[Real.cos (θ + 2 * π * k / n), Real.sin (θ + 2 * π * k / n)])
blocks.docstring:
The closed regular `n`-gon with center `c`, circumradius `r` and rotation angle `θ`: the convex
hull of the points `c + r • (cos (θ + 2πk/n), sin (θ + 2πk/n))` for `k = 0, …, n - 1`.
Every regular `n`-gon in the plane is of this form for some `c`, some `r > 0` and some `θ`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon`/`IsCcwConvexPolygon` (convex position only, no regularity), `Complex.exp`-based roots of unity (would require moving between ℂ and ℝ²).
justification.name: OuterBilliard.regularPolygon
justification.why_needed: No notion of a regular polygon (as a region of the plane) exists in Mathlib or the repo; needed for slot (ii). Defined as the convex hull of n equally spaced points on a circle with centre c, radius r, phase θ.

blocks.name: regularPolygon
blocks.text:
/--
The closed regular `n`-gon with center `c`, circumradius `r` and rotation angle `θ`: the convex
hull of the points `c + r • (cos (θ + 2πk/n), sin (θ + 2πk/n))` for `k = 0, …, n - 1`.
Every regular `n`-gon in the plane is of this form for some `c`, some `r > 0` and some `θ`.
-/
noncomputable def regularPolygon (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun k : Fin n =>
    c + r • !₂[Real.cos (θ + 2 * π * k / n), Real.sin (θ + 2 * π * k / n)])

@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem mem_rightSupportPoints_iff (P : Set ℝ²) (x v : ℝ²) :
    v ∈ rightSupportPoints P x ↔
      v ∈ P ∧ ∀ p ∈ P, (v 0 - x 0) * (p 1 - x 1) - (v 1 - x 1) * (p 0 - x 0) ≤ 0 := by
  have key : ∀ a b : ℝ², positiveOrientation.areaForm a b = a 0 * b 1 - a 1 * b 0 := by
    intro a b
    have h := triangle_area_eq_det a b 0
    simp only [triangle_area, vsub_eq_sub, sub_zero] at h
    simp [Matrix.det_fin_three] at h
    linarith
  simp only [rightSupportPoints, Set.mem_setOf_eq, key, WithLp.ofLp_sub, Pi.sub_apply]

@[category API, AMS 37 52]
theorem IsStep.unique {P : Set ℝ²} {x y y' : ℝ²} (h : IsStep P x y) (h' : IsStep P x y') :
    y = y' := by
  obtain ⟨-, v, hv, rfl⟩ := h
  obtain ⟨-, v', hv', rfl⟩ := h'
  rw [hv, Set.singleton_eq_singleton_iff] at hv'
  rw [hv']
blocks.docstring: The outer billiards map is single-valued where it is defined.

@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem isStep_unitSquare :
    IsStep {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1/2] !₂[1, 3/2] := by
  refine ⟨by simp, !₂[0, 1], ?_, ?_⟩
  · ext v
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_Icc, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩, h⟩
      have := h !₂[0, 1] (by simp)
      simp at this
      ext i
      fin_cases i <;> simp <;> linarith
    · rintro rfl
      refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
      rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
      simp
      linarith
  · ext i
    fin_cases i <;> simp [Equiv.pointReflection_apply]; norm_num
blocks.docstring:
Relative to the unit square, the outer billiards map sends the point $(-1, 1/2)$ to the point
$(1, 3/2)$: walking from $(-1, 1/2)$ towards the vertex $(0, 1)$, the square lies on the right.

@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem not_isStep_unitSquare (y : ℝ²) :
    ¬ IsStep {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] y := by
  rintro ⟨-, v, hv, -⟩
  have h₀ : !₂[(0 : ℝ), 1] ∈
      rightSupportPoints {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] := by
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
    rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
    simp
    linarith
  have h₁ : !₂[(1 : ℝ), 1] ∈
      rightSupportPoints {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] := by
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
    rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
    simp
    linarith
  rw [hv, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at h₀ h₁
  have := congrArg (· 0) (h₀.trans h₁.symm)
  simp at this
blocks.docstring:
Relative to the unit square, the outer billiards map is undefined at the point $(-1, 1)$, which
lies on the extension of the top side: the right support line from this point contains the whole
top side.

@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.i (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) :
    ∀ᵐ p : Fin n → ℝ², IsConvexPolygon p →
      ∃ o, IsOrbit (convexHull ℝ (Set.range p)) o ∧ ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range o) := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Unbounded orbits for almost every convex polygon.**
Outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits.

Precisely: for every $n \ge 4$ and Lebesgue almost every $n$-tuple of points
$(p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}) \in (\mathbb{R}^2)^n$ that are the vertices, in cyclic order, of a
(strictly) convex $n$-gon $P$, there is a point outside $P$ whose outer billiards orbit relative
to $P$ is well defined and unbounded, i.e. not contained in any bounded region of the plane.

Triangles are excluded: every triangle is affinely equivalent to a rational polygon, so all
outer billiards orbits relative to a triangle are periodic (Vivaldi–Shaidenko, Kołodziej,
Gutkin–Simanyi), and the claim for $n = 3$ is false. Since the outer billiards map is equivariant
under affine maps of the plane, the choice of parametrisation of convex $n$-gons by their vertex
tuples does not affect the meaning of "almost every".

Schwartz proved that outer billiards relative to any irrational kite (in particular the Penrose
kite) has unbounded orbits; kites form a null set of quadrilaterals, so the problem is open.

@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.ii (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) (hr : 0 < r) :
    ∀ᵐ x : ℝ², x ∉ regularPolygon n c r θ →
      ∃ o, IsOrbit (regularPolygon n c r θ) o ∧ o 0 = x ∧
        ∃ m : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic o m := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Almost every orbit is periodic for regular polygons.**
Outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

Precisely: for every regular $n$-gon $P$ (with $n \ge 3$), Lebesgue almost every point $x$ of
$\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus P$ has a well-defined outer billiards orbit relative to $P$, and this
orbit is periodic. Equivalently, the set of points outside $P$ whose orbit is undefined or not
periodic has Lebesgue measure zero.

The cases of the equilateral triangle ($n = 3$) and the square ($n = 4$) are trivial, since all
orbits relative to a rational polygon are periodic, and Tabachnikov settled the case of the
regular pentagon ($n = 5$). The problem is open in general.
blocks.name: outer_billiard.parts.ii

claims.decomposer_note: Read as: for each n, for Lebesgue-a.e. vertex tuple in ℝ^{2n} that is a (non-degenerate) convex n-gon P, some point of ℝ²∖P has a well-defined outer-billiard orbit (reflection through the right-hand support vertex, defined a.e.) that is not contained in any bounded set; note every triangle is affinely rational so all triangle orbits are bounded (Kolodziej, Gutkin–Simanyi), so the claim only makes sense for n ≥ 4 (or with 'almost every' interpreted so triangles are negligible), and the formalizer must fix that convention; affine invariance means the choice of parametrization/measure class is immaterial.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state essentially the same proposition (for every n ≥ 4, for Lebesgue-a.e. vertex tuple p : Fin n → ℝ² with the repo's EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon p, the convex hull admits a well-defined two-sided outer-billiard orbit with unbounded range), which matches the article's definitions (two-sided orbits, undefined where the support line contains a side) and Schwartz's convention (both forward and backward orbits defined and unbounded). c03 was chosen for its clean Set-valued definitions (rightSupportPoints / Step / IsOrbit), a uniqueness API lemma, and two concrete unit-square tests that verify both the sign convention and the undefinedness at side extensions. Edits: renamed Step → IsStep (and tests accordingly), lightly polished docstrings. c01 omitted `x ∉ P` from its step (harmless in effect but less transparent); c04/c05 use `![...]` against ℝ² which elaborates through `.ofLp` coercions (semantically fine, non-idiomatic); c05's IsRegularPolygon has a precedence bug allowing r = 0 in one disjunct; c07 shadows the repo's IsConvexPolygon with a bespoke one.
claims.source_text: showing that outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon have unbounded orbits
claims.text_span: showing that outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon have unbounded orbits

claims.decomposer_note: Referenced via 'Many problems concerning an outer billiard' (link to the article's open-problems list); for every regular n-gon P (n ≥ 3), the set of points of ℝ²∖P whose outer-billiard orbit is undefined or not periodic has Lebesgue measure zero; known for n = 3, 4 (rational, all orbits periodic) and n = 5 (Tabachnikov), open in general, so it is a co-equal question about periodicity, not a variant of the unbounded-orbit question.
claims.reviewer_why: For every n ≥ 3 and every regular n-gon (centre c, circumradius r > 0, rotation θ, which covers all regular n-gons), for Lebesgue-a.e. x outside the closed polygon there is a well-defined two-sided orbit through x that is periodic (∃ m > 0, Function.Periodic o m). This is exactly 'the set of exterior points with undefined or non-periodic orbit is null'; conditioning on x ∉ P is necessary since P has positive measure. Since the map is a partial bijection, 'eventually repeats' and 'periodic' coincide. c03's explicit parametric regularPolygon via `!₂[...]` is the most transparent; docstring edited to avoid the article's dubious 'only cases known' claim (the regular hexagon is affinely a lattice polygon).
claims.source_text: Show that outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.
claims.text_span: Show that outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

context: Outer billiards is a dynamical system based on a convex shape in the plane. Classically, this system is defined for the Euclidean plane but one can also consider the system in the hyperbolic plane or in other spaces that suitably generalize the plane. Outer billiards differs from a usual dynamical billiard in that it deals with a discrete sequence of moves outside the shape rather than inside of it.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Outer billiards

Outer billiards is a dynamical system defined relative to a convex shape $P$ in the plane.
For a point $x$ outside $P$, the outer billiards map sends $x$ to the point $y$ such that the
segment from $x$ to $y$ is tangent to $P$ at its midpoint and $P$ lies to the right of the ray
from $x$ to $y$. Equivalently, $y$ is the reflection of $x$ through the point where the right
support line from $x$ touches $P$. When $P$ is a polygon, the map is undefined at the points $x$
whose right support line meets $P$ along a side. The (two-sided) orbit of a point $x$ is the
sequence obtained by iterating the map and its inverse; it is well defined when every iterate is
defined, which is the case for almost every point.

An orbit is *bounded* if it is contained in some bounded region of the plane, and *unbounded*
otherwise. An orbit is *periodic* if it eventually repeats. Since the outer billiards map is
injective where it is defined, a well-defined orbit eventually repeats if and only if it is
periodic in the usual sense.

The Wikipedia list of unsolved problems in mathematics records "many problems concerning an
outer billiard, for example showing that outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon
have unbounded orbits". This file states this problem and the second open problem from the
open-problems section of the Wikipedia article on outer billiards: outer billiards relative to a
regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Outer billiard*, Open questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. E. Schwartz, *Unbounded orbits for outer billiards I*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702073)
- [S. Tabachnikov, *A proof of Culter's theorem on existence of periodic orbits in polygonal outer billiards*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1003)
-/

open EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory
open scoped Real

namespace OuterBilliard

/--
The points of `P` lying on the right support line from `x`: the points `v ∈ P` such that
all of `P` lies (weakly) to the right of the ray from `x` through `v`.

Here "to the right" is measured with the standard orientation of the plane: `p` lies to the right
of the ray from `x` through `v` when the signed area `areaForm (v - x) (p - x)` is nonpositive.
-/
def rightSupportPoints (P : Set ℝ²) (x : ℝ²) : Set ℝ² :=
  {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0}

/--
`IsStep P x y` means that `y` is the image of `x` under the outer billiards map relative to `P`:
`x` lies outside `P`, the right support line from `x` touches `P` in exactly one point `v`, and
`y` is the reflection of `x` through `v`. When the right support line from `x` meets `P` along a
segment, the outer billiards map is undefined at `x` and `IsStep P x y` fails for every `y`.
-/
def IsStep (P : Set ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  x ∉ P ∧ ∃ v, rightSupportPoints P x = {v} ∧ y = Equiv.pointReflection v x

/--
`IsOrbit P o` means that the two-sided sequence `o : ℤ → ℝ²` is a well-defined outer
billiards orbit relative to `P`: for every `k`, the point `o (k + 1)` is the image of `o k`
under the outer billiards map. Such an orbit is determined by any one of its points.
-/
def IsOrbit (P : Set ℝ²) (o : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, IsStep P (o k) (o (k + 1))

/--
The closed regular `n`-gon with center `c`, circumradius `r` and rotation angle `θ`: the convex
hull of the points `c + r • (cos (θ + 2πk/n), sin (θ + 2πk/n))` for `k = 0, …, n - 1`.
Every regular `n`-gon in the plane is of this form for some `c`, some `r > 0` and some `θ`.
-/
noncomputable def regularPolygon (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun k : Fin n =>
    c + r • !₂[Real.cos (θ + 2 * π * k / n), Real.sin (θ + 2 * π * k / n)])

/-- The right support points of `P` seen from `x`, in coordinates. -/
@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem mem_rightSupportPoints_iff (P : Set ℝ²) (x v : ℝ²) :
    v ∈ rightSupportPoints P x ↔
      v ∈ P ∧ ∀ p ∈ P, (v 0 - x 0) * (p 1 - x 1) - (v 1 - x 1) * (p 0 - x 0) ≤ 0 := by
  have key : ∀ a b : ℝ², positiveOrientation.areaForm a b = a 0 * b 1 - a 1 * b 0 := by
    intro a b
    have h := triangle_area_eq_det a b 0
    simp only [triangle_area, vsub_eq_sub, sub_zero] at h
    simp [Matrix.det_fin_three] at h
    linarith
  simp only [rightSupportPoints, Set.mem_setOf_eq, key, WithLp.ofLp_sub, Pi.sub_apply]

/-- The outer billiards map is single-valued where it is defined. -/
@[category API, AMS 37 52]
theorem IsStep.unique {P : Set ℝ²} {x y y' : ℝ²} (h : IsStep P x y) (h' : IsStep P x y') :
    y = y' := by
  obtain ⟨-, v, hv, rfl⟩ := h
  obtain ⟨-, v', hv', rfl⟩ := h'
  rw [hv, Set.singleton_eq_singleton_iff] at hv'
  rw [hv']

/--
Relative to the unit square, the outer billiards map sends the point $(-1, 1/2)$ to the point
$(1, 3/2)$: walking from $(-1, 1/2)$ towards the vertex $(0, 1)$, the square lies on the right.
-/
@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem isStep_unitSquare :
    IsStep {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1/2] !₂[1, 3/2] := by
  refine ⟨by simp, !₂[0, 1], ?_, ?_⟩
  · ext v
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_Icc, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩, h⟩
      have := h !₂[0, 1] (by simp)
      simp at this
      ext i
      fin_cases i <;> simp <;> linarith
    · rintro rfl
      refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
      rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
      simp
      linarith
  · ext i
    fin_cases i <;> simp [Equiv.pointReflection_apply]; norm_num

/--
Relative to the unit square, the outer billiards map is undefined at the point $(-1, 1)$, which
lies on the extension of the top side: the right support line from this point contains the whole
top side.
-/
@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem not_isStep_unitSquare (y : ℝ²) :
    ¬ IsStep {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] y := by
  rintro ⟨-, v, hv, -⟩
  have h₀ : !₂[(0 : ℝ), 1] ∈
      rightSupportPoints {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] := by
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
    rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
    simp
    linarith
  have h₁ : !₂[(1 : ℝ), 1] ∈
      rightSupportPoints {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] := by
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
    rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
    simp
    linarith
  rw [hv, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at h₀ h₁
  have := congrArg (· 0) (h₀.trans h₁.symm)
  simp at this

/--
**Unbounded orbits for almost every convex polygon.**
Outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits.

Precisely: for every $n \ge 4$ and Lebesgue almost every $n$-tuple of points
$(p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}) \in (\mathbb{R}^2)^n$ that are the vertices, in cyclic order, of a
(strictly) convex $n$-gon $P$, there is a point outside $P$ whose outer billiards orbit relative
to $P$ is well defined and unbounded, i.e. not contained in any bounded region of the plane.

Triangles are excluded: every triangle is affinely equivalent to a rational polygon, so all
outer billiards orbits relative to a triangle are periodic (Vivaldi–Shaidenko, Kołodziej,
Gutkin–Simanyi), and the claim for $n = 3$ is false. Since the outer billiards map is equivariant
under affine maps of the plane, the choice of parametrisation of convex $n$-gons by their vertex
tuples does not affect the meaning of "almost every".

Schwartz proved that outer billiards relative to any irrational kite (in particular the Penrose
kite) has unbounded orbits; kites form a null set of quadrilaterals, so the problem is open.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.i (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) :
    ∀ᵐ p : Fin n → ℝ², IsConvexPolygon p →
      ∃ o, IsOrbit (convexHull ℝ (Set.range p)) o ∧ ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range o) := by
  sorry

/--
**Almost every orbit is periodic for regular polygons.**
Outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

Precisely: for every regular $n$-gon $P$ (with $n \ge 3$), Lebesgue almost every point $x$ of
$\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus P$ has a well-defined outer billiards orbit relative to $P$, and this
orbit is periodic. Equivalently, the set of points outside $P$ whose orbit is undefined or not
periodic has Lebesgue measure zero.

The cases of the equilateral triangle ($n = 3$) and the square ($n = 4$) are trivial, since all
orbits relative to a rational polygon are periodic, and Tabachnikov settled the case of the
regular pentagon ($n = 5$). The problem is open in general.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.ii (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) (hr : 0 < r) :
    ∀ᵐ x : ℝ², x ∉ regularPolygon n c r θ →
      ∃ o, IsOrbit (regularPolygon n c r θ) o ∧ o 0 = x ∧
        ∃ m : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic o m := by
  sorry

end OuterBilliard

items: Outer billiards map: `Step P x y` requires x ∉ P, that the set `rightSupportPoints P x = {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0}` (points of P on the right support line from x) is a singleton {v}, and y = pointReflection v x = 2v - x. For a convex body P this is exactly the Schwartz/Tabachnikov/Wikipedia definition: y is the reflection of x in the right support point, undefined when the right support line meets P in a segment. The orientation convention ('P on the right' ⇔ areaForm ≤ 0 with the repo's standard orientation on ℝ²) was verified by the compiled test `step_unitSquare` ((-1,1/2) ↦ (1,3/2) via vertex (0,1)) and `not_step_unitSquare` (undefined at (-1,1), on the extension of the top edge). Using the left support line instead would give the inverse map, whose two-sided orbits are the same sets, so both conjectures are insensitive to this choice.

Orbits are two-sided sequences `o : ℤ → ℝ²` with `Step P (o k) (o (k+1))` for all k, following Wikipedia's definition ('iteratively apply both the outer billiards map and the backwards map'); 'well-defined orbit' = existence of such o. Schwartz's theorem indeed provides orbits defined and unbounded in both directions.
Unbounded orbit := ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range o), i.e. not contained in any bounded region (Wikipedia's definition).

Periodic orbit := ∃ m : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic o m. Wikipedia says 'eventually repeats'; because the outer billiards map is a partial bijection on the exterior of a convex body (the inverse is the reflection in the left support point), a well-defined two-sided orbit that eventually repeats is periodic in this sense, so the two readings agree.

'Almost every convex polygon' (slot i): parametrised, for each fixed n ≥ 4, by vertex tuples in Fin n → ℝ² with the product Lebesgue measure (`volume`, checked to be `Measure.pi` of Lebesgue on ℝ²), restricted via implication to tuples satisfying the repo's `IsConvexPolygon` (strict convex position in cyclic order, either orientation). Non-strictly convex tuples and relabellings are null/2n-to-1, so this is the natural measure class; affine equivariance of outer billiards makes the parametrisation choice immaterial.

Slot (i) is stated only for n ≥ 4 (decomposition notes require fixing this convention): every triangle is affinely rational, so all triangle orbits are periodic and the n = 3 instance would be false. The polygon P is the closed region convexHull ℝ (Set.range p).

Regular n-gon (slot ii): `regularPolygon n c r θ := convexHull ℝ (range fun k : Fin n => c + r • (cos(θ + 2πk/n), sin(θ + 2πk/n)))` with hypotheses 3 ≤ n and 0 < r; the statement is quantified over all c, r, θ so it literally covers every regular n-gon rather than only a standard one.

Slot (ii) a.e. condition: `∀ᵐ x, x ∉ P → ∃ o, IsOrbit P o ∧ o 0 = x ∧ periodic`, i.e. the set of points outside P whose orbit is undefined or not periodic is Lebesgue-null (as in the decomposition notes). Boundary points of P are null so x ∉ P vs x ∉ interior P makes no difference.
AMS tags 37 (dynamical systems) and 52 (convex geometry); both slots tagged `research open` (slot ii is known for n = 3, 4, 5 but open in general).

reviewer_notes: Modeling conventions (shared by all candidates and adopted): (1) 'almost every convex polygon' is read per number of vertices n, w.r.t. product Lebesgue measure on ordered vertex tuples in (ℝ²)^n, conditional on the tuple being a strictly convex n-gon in cyclic order (repo predicate IsConvexPolygon); the parametrization is finite-to-one and outer billiards is affinely natural, so the measure class is immaterial. (2) n ≥ 4 is imposed since every triangle is affinely rational and thus has all orbits bounded (Kolodziej, Gutkin–Simanyi); the n = 3 case is false, as the decomposition notes anticipated. (3) Orbits are two-sided and required to be defined at every iterate (the map is undefined exactly where the right support line meets P in a segment); this matches the Wikipedia definition and Schwartz's theorem statement. (4) Right vs. left convention only inverts the map and does not affect two-sided orbits, boundedness or periodicity; the sign convention was nevertheless checked by the unit-square test lemmas. Verified in Lean that `volume` on `Fin n → ℝ²` is the product of Lebesgue measures and that `Fin n → ℝ` coercions in regularPolygon elaborate as ((k : ℕ) : ℝ). Final file compiles with only 'declaration uses sorry' warnings.
